subject: SLA tolerance & runtime fallbacks for content-filter/tool-call failures
messages:
From: Laura Bishop <laura.bishop@acmehealth.com>
To: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.com>
Cc: Acme Health Procurement <procurement@acmehealth.com>
Date: Wed, 20 May 2026 11:02:00 -0400
Subject: Request: carve-outs for filter/tool failures in SLA

Neha —

Thanks again for the demo last week. Procurement has one outstanding ask before we finalize the contract: Acme Health runs regulated workflows that call external tools (document scanner, PII redaction tool) and rely on structured JSON output for our downstream ingestion. We’ve observed two classes of operational issues across vendors that we want explicitly addressed in the SLA:

1) Content filter false positives/blocking: when the content filter flags a request, the model call may be blocked or delayed pending human review. This causes apparent availability loss for our endpoints.
2) Tool-call failures / malformed structured output: when a called tool fails (timeout or 500) or the model emits invalid JSON, our pipelines experience backpressure and latency spikes.

We understand not all of these are the vendor’s direct runtime faults, but we need clear tolerance rules (what counts as an SLA breach vs an expected exception) and fallback obligations (automatic fallback to a safe model, conservative output, or queued retry with exponential backoff). Can you confirm Redwood’s position on:

- How a content-filter-induced rejection is classified for the 99.9% uptime commitment (is it a carve-out)?
- Whether tool-call timeouts count toward latency SLOs for hosted endpoints, and if Redwood will provide an automatic model-only fallback within X ms when a tool fails.
- Any credit / remediation policy if structured-output failures cause downstream ingestion errors for Acme (token costs and operational impact).

We’ve attached a short PDF that summarizes our procurement language and the redlines we’d propose. Can your team review and propose concrete SLA language we can use? We’re aiming to sign by end of next week.

Attachment: SLA_carveout_request.pdf (1 page)

—Laura
Laura Bishop
Head of Procurement, Acme Health
laura.bishop@acmehealth.com

From: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.com>
To: Laura Bishop <laura.bishop@acmehealth.com>
Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.com, marissa_cole@redwood.com, priyom_das@redwood.com
Date: Wed, 20 May 2026 11:25:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Request: carve-outs for filter/tool failures in SLA

Laura —

Appreciate the clear summary and the PDF. I’ve looped in Karthik (SE), Marissa (CS lead) and Priyom (legal) so we can give you a concrete redline quickly. High-level answers up front:

- Content-filter rejections: we typically treat system-level moderation blocks as an operational exception (carve-out) when the filter prevents request execution due to a prohibited content classification. We can add explicit language that distinguishes between (a) filter enforcement for disallowed content (carve-out) and (b) transient moderation service outages (not a carve-out).
- Tool-call timeouts: by default, third-party tool integrations are treated as downstream dependencies; latency from such tool-calls will be excluded from the hosted model latency SLO if the tool-call is invoked synchronously and fails in a way we detect as an external dependency error. However, we can commit to an automatic model-only fallback policy for the endpoints you specify (see below).
- Structured-output failures: we can define acceptance criteria (valid JSON schema + schema validation pass rate) and tie remediation credits to regression in those metrics.

Next steps: Karthik — can you draft a short appendix with the fallback behavior (time thresholds, which endpoints default to fallback, retry/backoff policy, and monitoring signals we’ll report)? Marissa — can you map how this would look in the Console (alerts, debug traces, example dashboards)? Priyom — please prepare a legal-friendly carve-out clause and a short template for DocuSign.

I’ll aim to get a draft back to you by tomorrow EOD. Attached: SLA_redlines_v2.pdf (initial working language).

Thanks,
Neha Kapoor
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference
neha.kapoor@redwood.com
+1 415-555-0132

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
To: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.com>, Laura Bishop <laura.bishop@acmehealth.com>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.com
Date: Wed, 20 May 2026 14:08:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Request: carve-outs for filter/tool failures in SLA

Hi all —

Picking up Neha’s ask with a proposed technical appendix. I’ll keep it short:

1) Classification rules:
  - "Filter enforcement" = when the moderation pipeline deterministically blocks a request due to policy match. Outcome: classified as a carve-out; counted as a valid rejection, not an availability breach.
  - "Filter outage" = when the moderation service returns 5xx / times out for the entire region. Outcome: treated as Redwood incident and counts toward uptime.

2) Tool-call handling (synchronous integrations):
  - If the tool-call does not respond within 500ms, Redwood will attempt a graceful fallback within 300ms of detection: first, return a model-only response (same model but without tool invocation), second, if model-only cannot satisfy the endpoint schema, return a standardized error payload with clear retry-after header.
  - We will surface a metric "tool_call_success_rate" and a per-endpoint counter for fallbacks.

3) Structured output validation:
  - We will validate JSON schema server-side for the endpoints you specify. Acceptance = 99.5% well-formed schema compliance over a rolling 30-day window. Breach remediation: service credit tiers tied to % below acceptance.

Notes: these times are conservative suggestions for hosted endpoints in us-west and us-east. If Acme wants stricter latency (e.g., 95th p95 under X ms including fallbacks), we can discuss dedicated routing or Reserved Dedicated capacity.

—Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
karthik_iyer@redwood.com

From: Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>
To: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.com>, Laura Bishop <laura.bishop@acmehealth.com>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.com
Date: Thu, 21 May 2026 09:05:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Request: carve-outs for filter/tool failures in SLA

Laura / Neha —

Thanks for the draft language. A few legal points and suggested wording for the carve-out clause:

1) Scope and definition: we should define "Content Filter Enforcement" and "Third-Party Tool Failure" explicitly, and limit carve-outs to cases where (a) the request is blocked because content violates an agreed policy, or (b) the tool is in the responsibility domain of the third-party integration and we can demonstrate via logs that the error originated in that external call.

2) Detection & Auditability: Redwood will provide audit logs (request id, timestamps, tool-call error codes) for any carve-out claim. Acme can raise a dispute within 30 days; cases will be triaged jointly.

3) Fallback obligation: Redwood agrees to implement the technical fallback behaviors described by Karthik for the specified endpoints. For avoidance of doubt, fallback activation (model-only, standardized error) will not be treated as an availability breach if it follows the documented detection rules.

4) Credits: propose a graduated credit schedule: minor regression (>=99% but <99.5%) = 5% monthly credit on the affected endpoint charges; significant regression (<99%) = 15% credit. Credits only apply to hosted usage and exclude third-party tool fees.

I’ve created a Jira ticket to track the implementation tasks and legal redlines: INF-2298. I can author the DocuSign-friendly clause and upload a clean SLA exhibit if everyone is OK with the above.

Attachment: SLA_redlines_v2.pdf (clean copy for legal).

—Priyom
Priyom Das
Senior Counsel, Redwood Inference
priyom_das@redwood.com

From: Laura Bishop <laura.bishop@acmehealth.com>
To: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.com>
Cc: Acme Health Procurement <procurement@acmehealth.com>, marissa_cole@redwood.com
Date: Thu, 21 May 2026 10:30:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Request: carve-outs for filter/tool failures in SLA

Neha / team —

Thanks — that level of detail is exactly what procurement needed. Couple quick follow-ups before we proceed: 

- Can we get the fallback activation latency guaranteed in writing (Karthik suggested detection + fallback within ~800ms total in the worst case). We’d like a committed upper bound for time-to-fallback so our downstream queueing guarantees hold.
- For the credit schedule, procurement would prefer a narrower band (e.g., 99.6% threshold for minor credits) — is that something you can accommodate in hosted pricing?

If you can update the exhibit with the exact numbers (time-to-fallback upper bound and the adjusted credit thresholds), we’ll get legal to sign and route DocuSign. Happy to take the final exhibit via the DocuSign link.

Cheers,
Laura
Laura Bishop
Head of Procurement, Acme Health
